sections.title: TCPA definition
sections.text:
Q: In your own words: what does TCPA (Time to Closest Point of Approach) measure?
A: TCPA is the time remaining, assuming both vessels hold their current course and speed, until the range between them reaches its minimum value (the CPA). It is a countdown to a moment in time, not a statement about whether a collision is happening.
(Why: Grounded in the tdgil.com CPA lesson: TCPA is computed as the distance from the current position to the CPA point divided by the relative speed -- it answers 'when', not 'is there danger'.)

sections.title: TCPA definition
sections.text:
Q: Does TCPA by itself tell you whether a collision risk exists?
A: No. TCPA only tells you WHEN the closest point of approach occurs. Whether that closest approach is dangerous depends entirely on CPA (how close), not on TCPA (how soon). A very small TCPA with a large CPA means 'passing safely very soon'; a very large TCPA with a tiny CPA means 'on a dangerous course, but not yet close'. You always need both numbers together.
(Why: This is the single most important corrective fact for the confirmed TCPA-misread error: TCPA answers 'when', CPA answers 'how close'. Neither alone answers 'is this dangerous'.)

sections.title: TCPA = 0
sections.text:
Q: A contact shows TCPA = 0 s and CPA = 5 m. What is happening right now, precisely?
A: Right now, at this instant, the two vessels are at their closest point of approach to each other, and that closest distance is 5 m. TCPA=0 means 'the closest point is occurring now', not 'a collision is occurring now' -- but because CPA is only 5 m here, this specific case genuinely is a high-risk, very-close-quarters moment.
(Why: TCPA=0 always means 'closest approach is now'; whether 'now' is dangerous depends entirely on the paired CPA value, which here happens to be small.)

sections.title: TCPA = 0
sections.text:
Q: True or false: 'TCPA = 0' always means a collision is happening right now.
A: False. TCPA = 0 means the closest point of approach is occurring right now -- it says nothing about the distance at that closest point. A collision requires CPA to also be essentially zero (the vessels' hulls actually coincide). TCPA=0 with CPA=500m is simply the moment two vessels pass each other with 500 m of clearance.
(Why: Direct true/false correction of the confirmed misread pattern.)

sections.title: TCPA small positive
sections.text:
Q: TCPA = 3 s, CPA = 1200 m. Closest approach has not happened yet -- it will happen very soon. Is this a collision right now? What should the agent expect in the next 3 seconds?
A: No, this is not a collision right now. The closest point of approach will occur in 3 seconds, and at that moment the minimum range will be about 1200 m. Given the large CPA, this is a routine, low-risk passing event soon.
(Why: TCPA=3s means the closest-approach moment is 3 seconds in the future, not now. Risk assessment (low) comes from the CPA value (1200 m), not from how small TCPA is.)

sections.title: TCPA large positive
sections.text:
Q: TCPA = 400 s (6.7 min), CPA = 150 m. How urgent is this right now?
A: Not urgent right now. The closest approach is still 6.7 minutes away. There is ample time to observe how the situation develops and to take early action per Rule 16 well before it becomes a close-quarters situation -- but the projected CPA of 150 m means this is worth continuing to monitor rather than dismissing, since a projection this far out is also more likely to change as both vessels' actual courses evolve.
(Why: A large TCPA means plenty of time remains; it does not mean the situation is unimportant if the projected CPA is tight, only that there's no need to react in the next few seconds.)

sections.title: TCPA negative
sections.text:
Q: TCPA = -5 s, CPA = 20 m. What does a NEGATIVE TCPA mean here, and what is the current situation?
A: A negative TCPA means the closest point of approach already happened, 5 seconds ago, assuming both vessels held course and speed since then. The minimum range reached at that moment was about 20 m. The vessels are now moving apart (diverging) rather than closing. This was a genuinely close call that has now passed. No avoiding action is needed now on the basis of this projection alone.
(Why: Negative TCPA is the mirror image of the main confusion: it does not mean 'collision already happened', it means the projected closest-approach moment is in the past, and (assuming the projection was accurate) the vessels are now opening range.)

sections.title: TCPA negative
sections.text:
Q: A contact's TCPA changes from +8 s to -3 s between two consecutive updates. What just happened?
A: The closest point of approach moment has just passed, roughly between those two updates -- the vessels were closing, reached minimum range, and are now diverging. This is an expected, normal transition as any encounter resolves, not itself an alarming event; what matters is what the CPA value was at the moment TCPA crossed zero.
(Why: Demonstrates TCPA crossing from positive to negative as a normal event marking the passing moment, not a fault or a new danger.)

sections.title: TCPA negative
sections.text:
Q: Should an agent ever treat a very large negative TCPA (e.g. -900 s) combined with a stale contact age as meaningful for current decision-making?
A: Generally no. A large negative TCPA means the projected closest approach was a long time ago under the course/speed assumptions of that projection. If the contact data is also stale (large age_s), the projection itself is unreliable -- the target has likely changed course or speed since, and a fresh bearing/range reading should be used instead of trusting an old negative-TCPA projection.
(Why: Connects TCPA sign interpretation to the broader point (raised earlier in this project, re: stale contact age_s) that old projections should not be treated as current fact.)

sections.title: Relative bearing convention
sections.text:
Q: State the sign convention this system uses for relative bearing.
A: relative_bearing = (true_bearing_to_target - own_heading + 540) % 360 - 180, giving a value in the range (-180, +180]. POSITIVE means the contact is on the STARBOARD side (clockwise from the bow). NEGATIVE means the contact is on the PORT side (counter-clockwise from the bow). 0 deg is dead ahead; +90 deg is the starboard beam; -90 deg is the port beam; +/-180 deg is dead astern.
(Why: This is the project's own established convention (used throughout narrate.py, colreg_llm_bridge_paused.py, evaluate_run.py) -- consistency with this exact convention matters more than which of several equally valid conventions is used, since the agent's own state data is generated with this one.)

sections.title: Relative bearing convention
sections.text:
Q: How does this system's signed convention relate to the 0-360 clockwise 'XXXR' notation used in classic radar plotting (e.g. tdgil.com's Bearings lesson)?
A: They are the same underlying angle, expressed two different ways. The 0-360 clockwise form (e.g. '045R' = 45 deg clockwise of the bow) maps directly onto this system's signed form: 0-360 values from 0 to 180 correspond to +0 to +180 here (starboard); 0-360 values from 180 to 360 correspond to -180 to -0 here (port). Converting: signed = (value_0_360 + 180) % 360 - 180.
(Why: Explicit bridge between the two representations, since converting between them is itself a place sign errors can be introduced.)

sections.title: Relative bearing calculation
sections.text:
Q: Own-ship heading is 000 deg. A contact's true bearing is 030 deg. What is the relative bearing (signed), and which side is the contact on?
A: Relative bearing = (30 - 0 + 540) mod 360 - 180 = 30 deg. Since this value is positive, the contact is on the starboard. (Equivalent 0-360 clockwise notation: 30R.)
(Why: Direct application of the sign convention: 30 deg > 0 -> starboard.)

sections.title: Relative bearing boundary cases
sections.text:
Q: A contact has relative bearing exactly 0 deg. Describe its position and state whether it counts as 'port' or 'starboard' in the strict sense.
A: This is dead ahead. At exactly 0 deg, the contact is neither purely port nor purely starboard -- it sits exactly on the boundary (dead ahead or dead astern), or exactly abeam if +/-90.
(Why: Boundary values (0, +/-90, +/-180) are edge cases where a strict port/starboard label doesn't cleanly apply the way it does for any other value; an agent should recognise these rather than force an arbitrary port-or-starboard answer.)

sections.title: Bearing notation conversion
sections.text:
Q: A radar-style bearing is given as 010R (0-360 clockwise notation, per the tdgil.com Bearings convention). Convert to this system's signed convention and state the side.
A: 010R converts to +10 deg in signed form (values 0-180 stay the same and are starboard; values 180-360 become value-360 and are port). The contact is on the starboard.
(Why: Conversion rule: signed = value_0_360 if value_0_360 <= 180 else value_0_360 - 360.)

sections.title: R+S=T formula
sections.text:
Q: Own-ship heading (S) is 090 deg. Relative bearing (R, this system's signed form) to a contact is +20 deg. Using the R+S=T rule (Relative bearing + Ship's heading = True bearing), find the true bearing (T) to the contact.
A: Convert R to 0-360 clockwise form first: +20 deg -> 20R. Then T = (S + R) mod 360 = (90 + 20) mod 360 = 110 deg.
(Why: Grounded directly in the tdgil.com Bearings lesson's R+S=T formula; note R must be in the 0-360 clockwise form for this formula, not the signed form -- another place a silent conversion error can creep in if not made explicit.)
